title: Spring Boot
description: Configuration per environment, bean lifecycle, transactions, proxies and JPA performance.
resumo: Profiles (`application-prod.yml`) override the defaults; `@ConfigurationProperties` + `@Validated` for typed settings.
Beans are singletons by default: never keep per-request state in fields.
Actuator: health, metrics and probes; expose only what you need. Flyway versions the schema; never edit an applied migration.
`@Transactional` rolls back on unchecked exceptions; checked ones need `rollbackFor`. Never call HTTP inside a transaction.
A caught inner failure still marks a shared transaction rollback-only — use `REQUIRES_NEW` per unit of work.
Proxies: self-invocation, private and final methods skip `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable` and `@Async`.
N+1: fetch join, `@EntityGraph` or projections; keep relationships LAZY; never fetch-join a collection with pagination.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** development uses a local database and a payment sandbox; production uses the real ones. And `@Value` strings scattered across the code are untyped and unchecked.

**Concept:** a profile is a named set of configuration: `application-dev.yml`, `application-prod.yml`, activated with `spring.profiles.active` (or the `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE` variable). The profile file overrides the default one. `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a prefix to a typed class or record, which `@Validated` checks at startup.

**How it works:** keep shared defaults in `application.yml` and only the differences in each profile file. Group related settings in one properties record instead of many `@Value` fields.
examples.interview_question: How do you separate dev, test and production configuration in Spring Boot?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Production secrets in a versioned profile file. Everyone with access to the repository has the password, forever (git history keeps it). Reference an environment variable or a secrets manager.
examples.code:
# WRONG: application-prod.yml in git
spring:
  datasource:
    password: S3cr3t!

# RIGHT
spring:
  datasource:
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}

subsections.subtitle: Bean Scopes and Lifecycle
subsections.formerSubtitle: Escopos e Ciclo de Vida de Beans
subsections.description: Singleton by default — so keep beans stateless.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a service keeps the "current cart" in a field, and two requests at the same time overwrite each other's data.

**Concept:** the default scope is singleton: one instance per application, shared by every request — and requests run on different threads. Other scopes: prototype (a new instance for each injection), request and session (web). Lifecycle: create, inject dependencies, run `@PostConstruct`, use, and run `@PreDestroy` on shutdown.

**How it works:** singleton beans such as `@Service` and `@Repository` must be stateless: no per-request data in fields. Request data travels as parameters or lives in the database or session.
examples.interview_question: What is the default scope of a Spring bean, and what care does it require?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Per-request state in a singleton field. Every user shares the same list, so one sees another's cart, and concurrent changes corrupt it.

subsections.subtitle: Spring Boot Actuator
subsections.description: Health checks and metrics, ready for production.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** in production, load balancers and Kubernetes need to know whether the application is alive and ready, and you need metrics — without writing those endpoints yourself.

**Concept:** Actuator adds operational endpoints under `/actuator`: `health` (UP or DOWN, including the database), `info`, `metrics`, `prometheus` (with `micrometer-registry-prometheus`), and the liveness and readiness probes. Over HTTP, only `health` is exposed by default.

**How it works:** expose what your platform needs and nothing more. Some endpoints reveal configuration and internals, so keep them unexposed or protected.
examples.code:
# application.yml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true   # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness

$ curl localhost:8080/actuator/health
{"status":"UP"}
examples.interview_question: What is Spring Boot Actuator for, and which endpoints are risky to expose?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Exposing every endpoint with `include: "*"`. `env`, `configprops` and `heapdump` reveal configuration and memory contents to anyone who can reach the application. List only what you need, and consider a separate internal port.
examples.code:
# WRONG: exposes env, configprops, heapdump...
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: "*"

# RIGHT
management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus
  server.port: 9090          # Actuator on an internal port, not exposed publicly

subsections.subtitle: Database Migrations with Flyway
subsections.description: Versioning the schema together with the code.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** someone adds a column on their machine, but test and production do not have it, and the application breaks on deploy. `ddl-auto=update` changes the schema implicitly, does not drop or rename columns correctly, and keeps no history.

**Concept:** Flyway applies versioned SQL scripts in order (`V1__`, `V2__`...) when the application starts, records which ones ran in the `flyway_schema_history` table, and leaves every environment with the same schema. Schema changes are reviewed in pull requests like any other code.

**How it works:** put the scripts in `src/main/resources/db/migration`; with the Flyway dependency, Spring Boot runs them at startup. Set `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate`, so Hibernate only checks that entities and tables match.
examples.code:
<!-- pom.xml: flyway-core, plus flyway-database-postgresql for PostgreSQL (Flyway 10+) -->

-- src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_orders.sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  total       NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- V2__add_order_status.sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'CREATED';
examples.interview_question: Why not use spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update in production?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Editing a migration that has already run. Flyway stores a checksum of every applied script and refuses to start when one changes. Never change an applied migration; add a new one.
examples.code:
-- WRONG: editing V2 after it ran
-- startup fails: "Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 2"

-- RIGHT: a new migration
-- V3__make_status_indexed.sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders (status);

subsections.subtitle: Transactions and @Transactional
subsections.description: Propagation, rollback rules and transaction length.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a method saves several things and fails halfway — sometimes everything is rolled back, sometimes not, and under load the connection pool runs dry.

**Concept:** `@Transactional` on a public method of a Spring bean opens a transaction, commits at the end, and rolls back on `RuntimeException` and `Error` — not on checked exceptions, unless you add `rollbackFor`. Propagation defines what happens when one transactional method calls another: `REQUIRED` (the default) joins the existing transaction, `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends it and opens a separate one. `readOnly = true` lets Hibernate skip dirty checking.

**How it works:** long transactions hold a pool connection and database locks for the whole time, which hurts concurrency — never make external HTTP calls inside one.
examples.interview_question: Why avoid long transactions, and when does a rollback happen?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Catching an exception from an inner `@Transactional` call and carrying on. With `REQUIRED`, the inner method shares the outer transaction and marks it rollback-only when it throws, so the outer commit fails anyway. Give each unit of work its own transaction.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a method has `@Transactional`, yet there is no transaction — and nothing in the logs says why.

**Concept:** Spring wraps the bean in a proxy, and the transactional logic runs when a call goes through that proxy. A call like `this.method()` inside the same class goes straight to the real object and skips the proxy — the same applies to `@Cacheable`, `@Async` and `@Retryable`. Private and final methods cannot be intercepted either.

**How it works:** move the annotated method to another bean, or reorganize where the transaction starts.
examples.interview_question: Why does a @Transactional method called from inside its own class not start a transaction?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: `@Transactional` on a private method. The proxy cannot intercept it, so the annotation is silently ignored. Use a public method on a Spring bean, called from another bean.

subsections.subtitle: JPA: N+1, Lazy and Eager
subsections.description: The most common performance problem with Hibernate.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a page lists 50 orders and fires 51 queries; in production, with 1,000 orders, it takes seconds.

**Concept:** N+1 happens when one query loads N entities and reading a lazy relationship on each one fires an extra query. Find it by turning on SQL logging or Hibernate statistics in tests. Fix it with a fetch join, `@EntityGraph` or a DTO projection. Keep relationships LAZY by default — including `@ManyToOne`, which is EAGER unless you say otherwise.

**How it works:** switching to EAGER is not a fix: it loads the relationship in every query, even where nobody needs it.
examples.interview_question: How do you detect and fix the N+1 problem?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A fetch join of a collection combined with pagination. Hibernate cannot page in SQL, so it loads every order and item and pages in memory — only a warning in the log. Page the ids first, then fetch those orders with their items.
